title: Medical Office Replacement Sourcing
name: Medical Office Replacement Sourcing
metaTitle: Medical Office Replacement Sourcing for San Francisco 1031 Exchanges
metaDescription: Medical office replacement sourcing for San Francisco 1031 exchanges, screening South San Francisco biotech overflow and Peninsula outpatient conversions.

sections.html: A medical office building runs nothing like a standard office floor, and anyone who has managed one for a physician group already knows it before a rent roll ever gets pulled. Negative-pressure exam rooms, backup power for refrigerated pharmaceuticals, and imaging equipment that can't tolerate an unplanned outage all change what downtime actually costs in this asset class, and that's exactly what we're screening for before a San Francisco building ever makes it onto an identification list. A broker's summary sheet won't tell you any of this, which is why we walk the mechanical rooms ourselves rather than relying on a marketing packet.

sections.heading: Why Physician Space Doesn't Behave Like Standard Office
sections.html:
Physician groups sign leases keyed tightly to their buildout, not the shell, so the tenant improvement allowance and amortization schedule usually run longer and heavier than a standard office deal. Electrical load, medical gas lines, and dedicated exhaust for procedure rooms are sunk into the space in a way that makes relocation expensive for the tenant, which is good news for lease durability but bad news if the systems behind those buildouts were never maintained on schedule.

Patient parking ratios also run higher than a typical office tenant needs, and a building that reads fine on an office parking count can fall short the moment it's leased to a group seeing forty patients a day. We ask for actual patient volume data rather than accepting a stated parking ratio at face value, since the two don't always line up in older buildings.

sections.heading: South San Francisco's Biotech Overflow Is Reshaping the MOB Pool
sections.html:
Life-science expansion in South San Francisco has pushed clinical and diagnostic tenants who can't secure space near the campuses out toward Redwood City and Walnut Creek, and that overflow is tightening availability in buildings that used to sit quietly at stable occupancy. A property that looked like a steady, unremarkable hold two years ago can now be sitting on real rent growth simply because the tenant pool competing for it has widened.

That shift also means older buildings are getting retrofitted for clinical use faster than the surrounding market expects, so a building's current use on paper isn't always a reliable guide to what it's worth as a medical asset today. We track which shells have already pulled retrofit permits, since that's often the earliest signal that a plain office building is about to reposition as clinical space.

sections.heading: The Building Systems We Check Before an Address Ever Makes the List
sections.html:
• backup generator capacity and documented run-time under full clinical load
  • condition and inspection history of medical gas and vacuum lines
  • certification records for any negative-pressure or isolation rooms
  • parking ratio measured against actual patient volume, not office-standard counts
  • elevator capacity and door clearances for gurney and wheelchair traffic
  • ADA compliance history, including any open corrective-action items

sections.heading: Matching Physician Lease Terms to the 45-Day Window
sections.html:
Physician group leases often carry long notice periods and buildout amortization clauses that make an early termination expensive for the tenant, which is a selling point for the seller but something we still verify line by line rather than take on faith. That verification has to happen inside the 45-day identification window, well before closing, since a lease that looks stable on a summary sheet can carry a renewal option priced well under market.

We keep the qualified intermediary looped in on timing from the start so exchange funds and closing documents move on the same schedule as the lease review, rather than one waiting on the other. A delay in either track tends to compound quickly once a physician tenant's own credentialing or licensing timeline gets pulled into the mix.

sections.heading: Where Peninsula Zoning Makes or Breaks a Conversion
sections.html:
A general office building in Redwood City or San Mateo can look like an easy medical-use conversion on paper, but Peninsula zoning treats clinical occupancy differently from standard office in ways that vary block by block. Parking overlay requirements and conditional-use permitting can add months to a timeline that an investor assumed would be routine, so we confirm zoning status with the local planning department before a conversion candidate goes anywhere near an identification list.

The distinction between an as-of-right clinical use and one that requires a conditional-use permit is the single biggest variable in how fast a conversion candidate can actually open, and it needs to be resolved before, not during, the exchange timeline.

faqs.q: What makes underwriting a medical office building harder than a standard office deal?
faqs.a: The building systems carry more risk if neglected. Backup power, medical gas lines, and negative-pressure certifications all need direct verification, since a lease summary won't tell you whether those systems have been maintained on schedule.

faqs.q: How is South San Francisco's biotech growth affecting medical office availability elsewhere in the region?
faqs.a: Clinical and diagnostic tenants priced out of space near the life-science campuses are moving into Redwood City and Walnut Creek, which is tightening availability and pushing rent growth in buildings that had been stable for years.

faqs.q: What backup power documentation should be reviewed before identifying a medical office building?
faqs.a: Generator capacity and a documented run-time test under full clinical load, rather than only a maintenance log. A generator that has never been load-tested at capacity is a real risk for a tenant running refrigerated pharmaceuticals or imaging equipment.

faqs.q: Do physician group leases complicate the 45-day identification window?
faqs.a: They can, since buildout amortization and long notice periods need to be verified against actual lease language rather than a summary. That review needs to happen inside the identification window, not after the property is already on the list.

faqs.q: Should a standard office building be identified with plans to convert it to medical use?
faqs.a: Only after zoning and conditional-use permitting are confirmed with the local planning department. Peninsula cities vary block by block on clinical occupancy rules, and permitting delays can eat into the exchange timeline fast.
